utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, you're to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It's true that we didn't do much last week. I will ask my case manager to put a document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good morning. Today we're going to discuss a few items that were in your statement, the statement that you read. I'm sure that you remember that you read your statement; the Prosecutor asked you if you did. Witness, please. Do you hear me? Do you hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have trouble hearing you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He's sitting far from the mic, so perhaps that's a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please have the witness's statement, 65 ter document 2889, and I would like to have page 3, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This document is part of your statement, and the Prosecutor asked you to read it last Friday. Do you remember having read it last Friday? Witness, please, on your screen, do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, but the print is very small. Maybe it's because of my eyesight.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Is it better now?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It is. It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So this is your statement, the statement that you gave the very day after the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, for purposes of clarity of the record, Ms. Isailovic has been asking the witness about "the statement the Prosecutor read to you last Friday." That was the witness's statement to a Tribunal investigator. This is a statement to the local authorities in Bosnia, just so that we have clear that the two statements are being a bit mixed up here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me explain what is going on exactly. The Prosecutor introduced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On the record, Mr. Docherty's last intervention has been attributed to me. I may benefit from the mistake, Mr. Docherty, but could that be changed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. So let me explain why I'm using this statement. It is part of document 2889 that the Prosecutor presented to the Tribunal through -- with the marking P162.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, while that is being done, my last statement was that Mr. Docherty's last intervention had been attributed to me, but the transcript says "Dragomir Milosevic's last intervention ..." It's Mr. Docherty's last intervention that was mistakenly attributed to me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, maybe the Prosecutor did not ask you to read this part of the statement, but do you remember that on the day after what happened on the tram you were driving, you talked to a policeman, the policeman who was in charge of what had happened to the tram at that time? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the date. I remember the date that I read. On that day, I drove a tram between Marindvor and the technical school and the Marshal Tito barracks. I was fired at between the two museums. On the left there were the four sky-scrapers and there was firing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement to that policeman, you said that the tram was shot at when you were -- and it's a technical word that I'm going to quote. I'm just waiting for the translation, because in French we would say that it's the place where the tram can actually take the curve but is still going straight. This is a section of the tram tracks where you can actually turn, and that's called the curve on the tracks.

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tram cut across. I headed to the right and then to the left and then towards the technical school.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. So when the tram is actually on that very spot on the tracks, isn't it noisy? Doesn't the tram make noise at that moment?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before the turn. I was shot at between the two museums, the revolution museum and the other one, and the street that goes from there towards Marindvor. I heard a shot. The passengers were screaming for me to turn and take shelter behind the revolution museum. There were two women who had been wounded. I don't know where they were taken to, whether there was an ambulance that came for them or whether they were taken to the hospital at Kosevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: My question, Witness, was the following: When the tram was on the tracks -- on the place where the tracks switch - you know, "aiguillage" in French - was there a noise at the time? I mean, you've been a tram driver for quite a while. When the tram actually takes that turn and is on the switch -- switching tracks, isn't it noisy?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand you. I was driving between the museums, the old museum and -- the road is there. I was on the road itself and that's where I came under fire. There is the fire sky-scrapers; right? The passengers started crying for help, and then I took shelter behind the museum of the revolution. I realised that the passengers had got off and they'd taken those two injured women away. I don't know where they took them to, whether it was an ambulance that took them away or what. I believe that it was an ambulance, and it was in the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, fine. Fine. But on the day after the incident, you made a statement to the police, and is that the truth? Did you really say what really happened on that statement?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just gave them my name from my travel order, the one I had on me, because I was driving the tram. They told me to go and to report the next day to the assembly. The assembly building was at Skenderija, just up from the Sremska Dzakovic Street, which used to be called Oslobodilaca Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, if I heard you well, the statement you made to the police, you made it in the assembly. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last name --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying the next day, not the day of incident but the next day. You went to the assembly to make the statement that is now on the screen. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I made an honourable statement and that's all I know. He said I should be off, I should go home, so I did and that's all I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask my case manager to call up the document 59 on the 65 ter list -- 159.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, about one month after this incident where your tram was shot at, a policeman made a report. Please wait for me to finish my sentence before you answer. So there's this report that was made by the police on December 15, 1994. In this report, it is said that a bullet went through the open window of your tram; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the window was open. I don't know who opened it. It certainly wasn't me. There was firing, and the glass shattered into a thousand pieces. There were several young men behind me and they were certainly the ones to open the window, and then the shot must have come through the open window.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard about the casualties that actually occurred in that tram incident?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just made a statement to them. There was a travel order with my name on it. They took my statement. A photographer came; he took photographs of the tram. And they told me to go home, which was at about 16 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Palo, would you listen me, please. What counsel was asking was whether you had heard anything about the people who were injured, the casualties on that tram. Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard nothing. I heard people moan and cry for help, but I was in a hurry to take shelter. There were wounded people on the tram and they took them off the tram, and I have no idea where they took them to, whether it was an emergency ward or the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, who told you to continue? As you said, there were wounded, but "Go on, go on," who said that to you?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told to drive on to the depot, to take the tram to Alipasin Most. And then a commission arrived later on, two police officers, a photographer, and another man who took my name, and they told me to go to the assembly building at Skenderija the next day. So I did. I gave a brief statement, and that's about the extent of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, my question is: Who told you, "Drive on drive on. There are wounded on board. Drive on." Who said that? Can you please give us a name?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of the passengers. They told me to take shelter behind the museum of the revolution because we couldn't be fired at there. As for the two injured ladies, they got off and they took them somewhere. I don't know where they took them to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, who told you that the shots came from the sky-scrapers in Grbavica? Who told you that that's where the shots originated from?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that with the naked eye. There are four sky-scrapers. The distance is 300 metres between the sky-scrapers and the positions, and that's where I came under fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, Witness, did you think that the only place that the shots could come from were those towers, those high-rises?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fire came from the left, but I have no idea where the shots were fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness, I will move to the statement you gave to the Prosecutor. You also had the opportunity to read this statement. This is 65 ter number 2889, and I'm looking at the second page. Witness, please, you've been a tram driver for quite a while. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have been a driver for 25 years.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not get the years that the witness mentioned. We apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just let the witness repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So regarding your experience in terms of tram driving, could you repeat when you started driving trams and the date you were finished with that job?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started on the 23rd of March, which is when we were called back to our company to drive trams. Between that time and the end of the war, I was driving trams, but it was very difficult. I would drive for five days and then not drive for another five and then drive for five and not drive for ten consecutive days, and I had to report to my company every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Who asked you to take up tram driving again? You were retired and you were asked to go back on the job. Who asked you to go back on the job?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The company board. They called us and they told us to drive the trams because there was no one else to do it, and the passengers had to get around, they said. We had to get the work done. It was very difficult. I would go home and go back to work without knowing whether I would actually be safe and still be alive the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, do you see your statement on the screen?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have my glasses on. It's difficult. I see some letters there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please enlarge the print, at least on the B/C/S side. Is it possible?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see better now?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's much better now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Around the middle of the page, there's a paragraph that is a bit longer than others. I'm looking at the fourth paragraph. Here it says that your company asked you to go back on the job even though you were retired, asked you to be available to drive trams, and it's also said that you were instructed not to abide by the signals and the traffic code. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. We were at the traffic light. I'm not sure if it was actually working. We passed all the traffic lights and we drove up behind those buildings so they wouldn't see us or fire at us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember if there were other objects involved in traffic at the time? I mean, this is a wide road that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a few other vehicles. People didn't have the courage to just walk around that area. That was an open area and nobody wanted to go, lest they were fired at.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But the tram was running. In your opinion, was it safer for the tram to run than for other vehicles?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tram was a very dangerous place. There were passengers there; sometimes 20, sometimes 30, sometimes 50 passengers on a tram. We would pull over at all the stops, all the sheltered stops. And then there was this building behind which we took shelter and then there was the entry to Marindvor. There was the stop at Skenderija. It was a tram line from Bascarsija that pulled over there behind those three sky-scrapers. That was on or way to Marindvor. The Zagreb Hotel was there. That's where the tram stop was. The passengers get on the tram, and we would be off to Marindvor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Throughout the war, and I think during your entire life, you lived in Bistrik; is that true?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: On the screen you can read this passage in your statement where you're talking about Bistrik. You are also mentioning the confrontation lines that separate the two warring factions.

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sky-scrapers, the old sky-scrapers first, and there was just the road between them, and then on the other side there was the sky-scraper of the revolution, a low building. We took shelter behind that one, because they couldn't shoot at us from the sky-scraper while we were there because we were lower down than the top of the sky-scraper.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you're still talking about the incident on the tram. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I was asking another question. However, I think that the answer you gave us had to do with the incident of November 23rd, 1994, when the tram was shot, because you were talking about the high-rises.

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They could have fired at us, but this was the safest place. This was between the museum and then there was that open area between the sky-scraper and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the other location.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but now you're saying that -- how was it right after the museum?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The openest -- Marindvor was the openest. There was Marindvor and Bascarsija, the executive council, and then on the way back, the Zagreb Hotel. It was the best shelter. And you didn't have any other shelters on the way to the museum.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: At the time did you think that the only place possible to shoot to the tram is from the sky-scrapers? Is that what you were thinking at the time, that it was only from those sky-scrapers that the tram could be shot at?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have fired at us on our way through Marindvor. He could have fired at us from Debelo Brdo, the Jewish cemetery. Those would have been the best places for him to shoot at. We were in the palm of his hand. No shelter whatsoever. The walls were nearly destroyed and there was no shelter whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please. Witness, I wanted to ask you a question about Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Debelo Brdo yourself.

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Jewish cemetery, Debelo Brdo, you know where that is. That was the openest route possible. He could have used just an ordinary rifle. It didn't even require a sniper rifle. There was no shelter at all, and that's where I had to take my tram through.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So as a long-term resident of Sarajevo, I'm sure you know all those hills. Did you know that at the time the units of the BiH army were holding Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Debelo Brdo, I know that place. I know the Jewish cemetery. I know Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, in your statement, when you say -- could you please look at your statement on the screen, Mr. Witness. On the screen, there is your statement, and you say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel and witness are overlapping. It is impossible to continue with the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Mr. Palo and Ms. Isailovic, the interpreter complains that you are both overlapping. Mr. Palo, please observe a pause between the question and the answer. Do you understand? Don't speak at the same time as counsel is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, this is one last question and then we'll wrap up. On the screen you have --

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the screen in front of you? On that screen there is your statement and the words --

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also wish to add, we were ordered not to observe traffic lights. They hardly ever worked, but we were ordered just to go through regardless of what the light was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not understand the rest of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a bit further down in your statement, there is one sentence that starts with "Takodje zelim ..."?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would add that I live in the area of Bistrik. I don't know about those shells that were falling. I don't remember that. But they were falling. One fell. One fell. I mean, a tank could have stood there, stopped there --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You also talk about confrontation lines because you're talking --

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... were further off in the hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in your statement.

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to read this now. Should I read the next paragraph or should I go back from the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now that we found the paragraph, this is my question: You knew -- did you know that on Debelo Brdo, the BiH units were stationed? Did you know that? Let me repeat my question: Did you know that on Debelo Brdo, which is a hill that you know well, there were units from the BiH army? And you say that in your statement at the last sentence of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our armies were under the hill, at the foot of the hill, and the Serb armies were up on the hills. We were totally surrounded and we had nowhere to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Are you also saying that for Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Debelo Brdo, Jewish cemetery, all of that was linked up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you also know Colina Kapa? It's also a peak on Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Colina Kapa. We got wood from there. There were big forests there and we would cut timber wood so that we could get some heating. There was no other way to get heating.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please wait for the witness to finish, notes the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, the interpreter asks that you wait until the witness has finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, do you remember that on that hill, the Colina Kapa hill on Trebevic, there were BiH units that were stationed there? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Our army was at the foot of the hill, Colina Kapa, underneath Debelo Brdo. I couldn't go up on the hill. That's where the Serb armies were.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And when you say in your statement that "our confrontation lines were a bit further higher up on the mountain," which mountain do you mean?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Debelo Brdo is very well known. I go there every other day by that hill, to the right, to the right of the road where our bus goes, our mini-van, that transports passengers. Then Zlatiste was there, Curine Njive, and then all the way up to Dzidzikovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement when you say "further up the hill," which hill were you thinking of, please?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know where the hill is. I didn't go up that hill. There's a village up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This is my last question. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was my last question. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the day the incident occurred, the day the tram was shot at, as far as you know, how many investigations were carried out on that day?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 23rd of March is when it started. We were called to the company and we were told that we had to work; that there was no one to drive the trams, that passengers had to be transported, that the army has to be on the lines. And there is nothing more I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But the day you were shot at, did the authorities come and conduct an investigation to see what had happened to your tram?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two policemen came, a man came, and a photographer came. They told me that I was being taken to the so-called garage where trams would be left. And they came and they looked at the number on the travel order and they told me to report to the assembly at Skenderija on the following day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And you were asked on the next day, who had shot at the tram, or did nobody ask you that question? Did somebody actually ask you that question?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was shooting, but I just know that it came from the left side, the bullet did, from the sky-scraper -- well, not from the Jewish cemetery. From the sky-scraper. It was nearby; 200 metres away from the sky-scraper to the tram line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The investigators who put questions to you, did they talk about potential snipers?

utterances.speaker: HUSO PALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police did not ask me. No one from the police asked me. They just took my name and surname and told me to report on the following day at Skenderija, at the assembly, at 10.00. I went there. There was a man there and, I don't know, he asked me a bit, not too much, and he told me to go home. After a few months, on the 15th of November, my son was wounded. That's when I was supposed to report at the Minister of the Interior to make a statement. I went there and I said that my son had been wounded and that I couldn't give any statement, and they said, "Okay. We know you. Go home and we'll call you later." A few months went by. I was called again. And there was a woman there and then a man, and there was a girl who was interpreting. And that was it until Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Huso Palo -- Mr. Palo, I'm addressing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That constitutes your evidence. We thank you for giving it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. All the best to you. I told you whatever I knew. I don't know more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before the next witness is brought in, may I just make two announcements. The first is that on Wednesday morning we'll have a hearing on the Prosecution's motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts. I'm allocating one hour for this hearing; 25 minutes for each party and 10 minutes for reply. And the parties are to concentrate on areas of difference between them. That's Wednesday morning, the day after tomorrow. And then I'd like to go into private session. Wednesday morning, it's 9.00

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness will be called by my colleague, Ms. Edgerton. At this time may I ask to be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness is here, so let him make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit. And you may begin, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for your reference before we begin, I should note that this witness will testify as to events that occurred on March 3rd, 1995, referred to in our schedule by the reference number SN-14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Could you tell us your name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Alen Gicevic is my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what's your present occupation?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I work as an economist in a company that is now privately owned.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I wonder if I could ask if we could pull up a series of documents on e-court, the first bearing the PT number 02899. That document exists in two languages. There's an English and a B/C/S version. 2899. Perhaps while we're waiting for that I could ask

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Prior to your testifying here today, did you have an opportunity to review two statements given by you to members of the Office of the Prosecutor, the first in 1996 and the second in 2006?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And were those statements made available to you in your language as well as the English language?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I apologise for this, Your Honour. There seems to be some trouble in locating the material in my colleague's folder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, when did you say that the first statement was given, in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 15 November 1996, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Or 1995? Could you check that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My mistake, Your Honours. 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Again, I'm loathe to proceed, even with the few additional questions I have, without the witness having the opportunity to have his statement in front of him, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, he should have it in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My colleague, Ms. Bosnjakovic, is re-sending the documents to the court officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe we can assist. On our list and in our exhibits we also have that document, so maybe we could assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Any way in which you can assist the process would be very much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we'll pull it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see the Serbo-Croatian translation. Can we manage to have the English on the other side, please, because the English is the one that the witness actually signed. Wonderful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gicevic, did you have an opportunity to review both of these document, the English one and the B/C/S one, prior to your testifying today?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the English one, I take it you recognise your signature on the document.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do you recall whether this document was read back to you in your own language before you put your signature to it?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall clearly whether it was read out to me in the Bosnian language, this document, when I gave this statement actually in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, can we go to the subsequent document which bears the number PT 02900, which is the second statement of this witness. I note my colleagues from the Defence team are assisting again, and I'd like to indicate my thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So would I.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, on the screen in front of you, Mr. Gicevic, you have copies in English and B/C/S of this statement from 21 April 2006. You've had an opportunity to review both of these documents before testifying today?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, prior to making this second statement in 2006, did you have an opportunity then to review the translation of the 1996 statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before making my second statement, I was given the statement that I had made ten years before.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, as a result of that review, did you find inaccuracies in the 1996 statement which you then corrected in this statement from last year?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I found three or four minor discrepancies and I indicated that to the investigator. That was then changed in the statement I gave last year, or, rather, the year before last.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, was this statement from 2006 either read back to you or translated in your own language before putting your signature to it?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: When I gave the second statement, I waited for an hour until the investigator compiled a note in the English language, then the translator wrote this in the Bosnian language, and then I had the opportunity to see both before I signed the English statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, then, together, do these two statements constitute an accurate record of what happened to you on March 3rd, 1995, which would be your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we then have those statements, the first from 1996 -- 1995, my apologies again, bearing the number PT 02899, and the second one bearing the number PT 02900, marked as exhibits, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first statement will be Exhibit P163, and the second, Exhibit P164.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, relating to those two statements and the events of March 3rd, perhaps you could answer some additional questions for us, and I'll begin, if I may. First, could you clarify in which direction the tram on which you were riding when you were shot was heading?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: The tram was going from east to west, from the new part of town to the old part of town, the centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And which side of the tram car were you standing on while you were riding in that direction?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I was just behind the middle part, next to the third door on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And from where you were standing, could you tell us what you could see? What was your point of view?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: To the right there was Grbavica, the Jewish cemetery, and the southern part of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. Just to clarify the witness's explanation here. Good morning, Mr. Witness. It seems to me that if you were driving towards the old town and you had Grbavica on your right, then you would have been driving from west to east; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because I think your statement was maybe incorrectly translated or confused somehow. But I think you said before that it was from east to west.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was going from the new part of town to the old part of town. As for the cardinal points, it is still my position this is west to east.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, perhaps with your hand, could you just touch the location on your body where you were hit and show the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For the record, the witness is standing and indicating with his right hand an area above his right knee.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And tell us, Mr. Gicevic, was there an exit wound?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: No. There was only the entry wound.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps now we could move on to a map which bears the number 02872 and display that on the screen, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gicevic, do you see this map on the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have the right-hand side of the map magnified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Gicevic, using the tool on the monitor in front of you - it's an electronic marking tool on the right-hand side - could you mark on this map, to the best of your recollection, where the tram was at the time that you were shot.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, could you put a small number 1 beside that.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, still looking at this map, could you mark for our benefit where you think the shots on the tram might have come from.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've made two lines from the bottom of the page of the map pointing towards what you've marked as number 1, the area the impact; one location you've marked as number 2 and the second location you've marked as number 3. Perhaps I could ask you a couple of questions about the first location, number 2. Could you tell us what sits at that location?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Location number 2 is a sky-scraper, 12 or 13 floors. It is just next to the Miljacka river.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And are you in a position to give us an estimation as to how far location number 2 is from location number 1 on this map?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe 400 to 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And are you aware of what sits at the location you've marked as number 3 on the map?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: There's another tall building there, seven or eight floors.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that seven- or eight-storey building, is it known by any name in particular?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: That building goes by the name of Metalka.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could you give us an estimation as to how far the Metalka building, which you say is location number 3, is from location number 1 on the map?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: It's roughly the same distance. Perhaps slightly further away. About 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, perhaps if you could mark one more thing for us on this map, if you're familiar with it, could you mark the location of the front line in that area.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could you mark the location of the front line, then, with the number 4, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With the number 4, I think, because you have already used up 1, 2 and 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if we could have this marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P164.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask the witness if he had any particular reason for saying that the shots came from the direction that he marked on the map, and whether this was a view that he formed at the time of the incident or subsequent to the incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those were buildings that were used to fire from before, across the Miljacka river. I can only speculate that that was where the bullet had come from, because those were two locations that were clearly visible from the tram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Mr. Witness, can I ask you whether your assumption was that the shot came from either one or the other of the two locations which you have indicated, or are you suggesting that there were two shots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say it was one or two. As far as I remember, there were two or three shots. Where they were fired from is not something that I can possibly know, whether it was from one place, one location, or from several different locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Provided that the image on the screen of the marked map is saved as the next exhibit, could we then move on to a further item bearing the number PT 02914. That's a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that on the document list, documents that are going to be used today, on the list that we received on the 30th of January, 2007, this particular photograph was not included, so unfortunately I was not able to prepare any discussion on that particular photograph. I was unable to do so, more specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, it may not have been included on the list, Your Honour. It's my understanding from my colleague Mr. Docherty that the photographs were handed over to Ms. Isailovic. In any case, Your Honours, given that is merely an enlargement, more panoramic view, of a photograph which appears in Your Honours' map books, I'm wondering if, indeed, there is an issue on the part of my friend Ms. Isailovic with respect to the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, assuming that you're correct, it looks as if you'll have the break, the first break, to do some preparation on that. I'll cause investigations to be made as to what the factual situation is. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Gicevic, among other things, does this photograph depict the location at which your tram came under fire on March 3rd, 1995, during which you were injured?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask you to take the marking tool again on the right-hand side of the monitor and mark that location for our benefit with the number 1, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, then, the locations you have identified on the previous map as number 1 and number 2, could you mark those on this photograph with the same numbers. Sorry, 2 and 3, I correct myself.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And finally, to be consistent with the map which you earlier marked, could you indicate the front line as you understood it to be and mark that with the number 4.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could have that marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P166. And, for the record, I wish to clarify that the previous map that was marked is, in fact, Exhibit is P165 and not P164, as I had indicated. I do apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if I understood you well, number 1 is the place where the tram was when you were hit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My last question is the following: What do the tram tracks look like? Are they in a straight line or are they curved so that the tram can turn into another direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was just past that place of the incident that the tracks turn from the left side of the street to the right side of the street. Rather, there is this area running down the middle of the street and the tracks at one point move onto the right side of the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would it assist Your Honours if the witness was able to indicate this on this latest exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]. [Interpretation] That would be the direction the tram was moving, or, rather, the tracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have that marked with the number 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Noting for the record that the line on this photograph marked number 5 indicates the curve in the tram tracks, approximately, which Judge Mindua was inquiring about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P167.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gicevic, earlier on in your testimony, referring to locations number 2 and 3 on this photograph - and, for the record, I note that was on page 28, approximately line 19 - you indicated there used to be dangers, sniper fire from these two locations. Now, perhaps I could ask you this: During the course of the war, in particular 1994 and 1995, did you have occasion to travel along the same route in front of these two locations?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I passed there on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, passing there, perhaps you're in a position to tell us about any measures you might have observed at those locations in order to protect the population, or along that route, in order to protect the population from those locations?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: This route as well as the route running parallel to this one behind the buildings had huge transport containers placed at some places that were deemed to be risky, as well as old lorries filled with sand. There were UNPROFOR soldiers at these risky places using their APCs to protect Sarajevo's population from the snipers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, perhaps I can just go back to what you were saying about the route parallel to this one. Would you be in a position to mark that on this photograph with the number 6 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. And even though we're on a new exhibit, I'll keep the consecutive numbering.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've also mentioned containers or lorries, transport containers or old lorries filled with sand. Were these scattered along these locations or were they laid in some kind of pattern, end on end? Were they grouped at all?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: They were across to the south, down the road, and I can mark that for you, our position at the time. This is how it was, roughly speaking. They were placed across, two or three long and three or four deep, along the tracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, could you please put the number 7 at the location which you've marked.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And were these containers on the north side of the road or the south side of the road; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Looking from here, they were in front. The road was -- so the containers were a form of physical protection for the citizens' vehicles and trams moving about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were there any other locations as depicted or in this photograph where you recall containers being placed?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of these two streets at this intersection that you've just indicated with the number 8?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: This is the so-called "Route of Life" and the junction was called "at the railway station."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the big white expanse in this photograph where you have written the number 8, what stood at that location at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: That was the old barracks, the old JNA barracks. That's where UNPROFOR was stationed in the war and just after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us what intersection we find at number 9.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Number 9, yes, there's a junction there; St. Mary's church and the "Route of Life" or the "Salvation Route." But there were many junctions there and it would take a lot of different numbers for me to mark them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you remember speaking about the UNPROFOR APCs you mentioned? Do you remember locations that you may be able to indicate on this photograph, locations where they were generally constantly placed?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indicated on the photograph as numbers 10, 11 and 12, Your Honours. If we could have that marked as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P168, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note the time, but I also note I have perhaps five minutes of questions for this witness. I'm in your hands as to when you would like to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gicevic, do you have any recollection of having observed or heard any fighting or military activity going on in the surrounding area on the day you were shot?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were two or three peaceful days. I am certain that no firing was to be heard on that particular morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were you on any kind of military service at the time of this incident?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, was this the only time you were injured during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could you tell us when this other occasion was? When were you otherwise injured?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I was injured again on the 22nd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What caused the injury then?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: The injury occurred at about 8.00 p.m. near my house, the house in which I was living with my parents at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And perhaps I can repeat the question: How was the injury caused?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I was injured by a shell. I received injuries to my leg and to my stomach. It was a mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To your recollection, was that the only shell that fell around the time you were injured on this first occasion?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: No. There were several shells. As far as I remember, in those moments there were three shells that landed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you note this happened near your house. Could you tell us where your house was at this time?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Dzidzikovac Street, at Mejtas.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what area of the town of Sarajevo was that?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: This is Sarajevo's centre. That is now a residential area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. You're a very fortunate man, and we are glad that you are here. We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, you're still on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Only briefly, Your Honour. With respect to the issue of notice of the photograph, Your Honour, I have made some investigations and I want to put my apologies on the record. I certainly had no intention of misleading anyone. The photograph, 2914, that my friend had said was not on the list, indeed, was not on the list and doesn't seem to have been passed to her previously. There was miscommunication, or perhaps too many communications over too many photographs, and there was -- while I understood she had received, she hadn't received it. We've discussed the photograph, I've passed her hard copies of the photograph, and I feel I should, with respect to this photograph, put on the record that this is a still drawn from a DVD of panoramic photographs of Sarajevo which sits on our list at PT 2716. And the photographs in Your Honours' map book, numbers -- sorry, I have to put my glasses on to read the numbers. The aerial photographs in Your Honours' map books, aerial number 2 and number 3, are in fact all drawn from the same DVD. But, nevertheless, my apologies for the misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. If Ms. Isailovic has been in any way embarrassed by that, she is to let the Chamber know we'll find a way to deal with it, perhaps by allowing her a little more time to cross-examine. But I note that she did have the break. But that's a matter you should bring to our attention, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. So that is an issue we have settled now. It wasn't necessary to apologise in such a manner. During the break, I looked at the photograph again, and I shall begin my cross-examination with this photograph. I believe it is on the screen already. Is that right? Does everybody have this photograph on their screen? I have it on my screen, any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. My name is Mrs. Isailovic. I'm a member of the Paris Bar Association, and I defend Mr. Dragomir Milosevic, charged before this Chamber. I shall now begin my cross-examination, as is customary here, and I shall ask you a few questions that pertain to your statements which we mentioned earlier this morning and a few additional questions which have to do with what you know about the situation in Sarajevo during the period for which the accused is charged in the indictment. I would like you to look at the photograph once more. This photograph is on our screens now. With the pen, could you show us where the confrontation or separation line was between the two warring factions. That is what it was called, anyway.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, is it fair to say that the confrontation line includes the units of both warring factions on both sides of this line?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I shall repeat my question. This line, this line you've just drawn which we have called the separation line between the two warring factions, according to you, does that line separate the two war factions; one faction on one side of the line and the other on the other side of the line?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: That was the separation line. But where the armies actually were, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Nonetheless, you knew that the soldiers of the Republika Srpska were positioned in the towers and the high-rise buildings which you indicated to the Trial Chamber today, and they were also positioned in the Metalka building, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I just said that the bullet could have come from the Metalka building. But whether the army was on top of the building, I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If that's what you say, would you also say between this line and the tracks of the tramway in which you found yourself on the 23rd of March, could there have been units of the ABiH in that short or small space?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Not likely.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Are you quite sure, or is it just something you have heard about?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Since this is a big expanse, empty space, it is logical that there should be no military facilities there or military forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you are talking about an open space, an open square, but I see here two buildings that are located between this line and the tram tracks which we saw a while ago. I stand to be corrected, of course.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the country museum is. Yes, there are two buildings there, the museum and the faculty of philosophy, in a relatively large area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you have shown us a lot of things on this photograph, and this is a clear indication that you know this area pretty well. Even if you were 34 years old at the time, you were not an ABiH soldier at the time, were you? Did I understand you right?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: At that moment, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, before you continue, just let me take the witness, very briefly, back to his evidence that, "as there was a big expanse, empty space, it is logical that there should be no military facilities there or military forces." Just to be clear, why do you say that it is logical that there be would no military facilities in a big expanse and empty space?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because there were two police stations on the left-hand side and on the right-hand side in the immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But are you now agreeing that there were, in fact, two buildings there, the museum and the faculty of philosophy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, a few moments ago you said to us that you were not a soldier at that time. Could you just expand on this a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was demobilised nine months before that, in July 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In your second statement, in your statement which bears the number 2900 on the 65 ter list, number P164.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like this to be displayed on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we're waiting for it. Is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, the photo that was just marked is not in evidence. Do you want to have it admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was just telling the usher that I did not wish to tender this photograph. It was just because I wanted to discuss it with the witness. I would like my case manager to turn to the third page now, please, paragraph 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you see this on your screen? Can you see your statement on the screen which is before you? And in paragraph 10 you mention the fact that you were involved in the Bosnian army. What interests me is this: You worked as a driver when you were requisitioned by the army. Did this occur after your demobilisation or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, nine months after my demobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Was that perhaps the time when you had your accident, on the 3rd of March, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was demobilised on the 20th of July, 1994, that is to say, nine months earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But when did you actually work as a driver and when were you requisitioned by the ABiH army? When was that?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: No, the army did not call me up. I myself showed up in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly? You were saying that after your demobilisation in July 1995 you were not part of the ABiH army; is that right? Is that what you are trying to say?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what you mean. You keep talking about mobilisation or demobilisation in 1995. I was a member of the army from 1992 to 1994. In 1995, when I was wounded, I was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement, in paragraph 10, I want to make sure that everything is quite clear. You say that until the summer of 1994 you worked in the army and you were a medical assistant. And then the second sentence in the paragraph numbered 10 reads as follows: "I also worked in the army as a driver when I was required to do so." This is a very simple question: After the summer of 1994, were you asked to act as a driver by the ABiH army?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: No. From 1992 until 1994, first I worked as a male nurse and then as a driver. On the 20th of July, 1994, I severed all links to the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Things are much clearer now. I should now like to get back to what happened on the 3rd of March, 1995. I would like to say that we heard in this courtroom the tram driver who came to testify, and the tram driver explained to us what happened during the incident. This is in the transcript on page number 867, the 23rd of January, 2007. The woman who was the driver of this tram talked to us about the time when the accident occurred, and she told us that it was when the tram reached the second turn. You did answer the question put by the Prosecutor. There are two turnings, two curves, one which turns to the right and the other which turns to the left. And the driver explained that the first part of the tram crossed or went past the second curve and that is when the accident occurred. Do you agree with this? Do you know anything about this? Do you know when the tram was hit?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: When the tram track goes from one side of the street to the other side of the street, it's only 5 or 6 metres, and it takes the tram only a second to cross that street, from one side to the other. So I really don't know at what moment that was. When the shooting started, we all fell, on the one hand because the tram swerved and on the other hand because bullets started flying.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement, you mentioned two or three bullets. Are you quite sure?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot be 100 per cent sure because it was all very nearby, so I could not tell what the actual firing was, what the actual bullet was, so that's why I said rather imprecisely two to three.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could there have been only one bullet that hit the tram?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Nonetheless, Witness, after what happened, the Bosnian police conducted an investigation, and someone contacted you also. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Before discussing this police investigation, I would like to turn to the second page of the document we have in front of us. In the third paragraph of this statement, you corrected a few mistakes that were in there. I'm talking about your first statement which you gave on the 15th of November, 1995. The second statement we have is the statement which was given nearly 11 years after the fact. So you corrected your 1995 statement, and you explained how it was that you went to hospital. This is in paragraph 3; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that at the time you were wounded, you left the tram of your own accord. You didn't address yourself to the tram driver and you didn't address yourself to the policeman who was there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I did not address anyone because there was panic all over. When a bullet hits you, you do not go to the tram driver; you go to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But I believe that you were very seriously injured, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Much less serious than the first wound, so I was calm and composed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you then tell me how the police discovered that you were a passenger on the tram on the day that the tram was hit?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand at all who it was that I was making statements to. I made a statement much later, not at the moment when I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, that is precisely why I'm putting this question to you. Let's assume that all this happened. You leave that spot without addressing yourself to anyone, and after that, people understand that you were a passenger on that tram. Could you tell me what happened? And how did you contact the police? Admittedly, the police did cross-question you but that was somewhat later.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived hospital, the State Hospital, there were always representatives of the media there, and as I was entering the hospital in order to be treated, there were TV crews there and radio crews and they asked me what it was that happened and I said that I was hit in a tram. That is probably where it all started from. I did not look for anyone to make a statement to, and it was only later that this happened with the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to check something. You were greeted by the media when you are reached the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I was not greeted by the media. At Kosevo and at the State Hospital there was always someone, because somebody was injured every day, so that is where they gathered information about casualties, about the dead and wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Were the media already aware of what had happened or did you pass on the information?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: From the hospital I couldn't have known who it was who had brought that information, but I know, at any rate, that it was on the TV news that evening, immediately, that a tram had been hit by a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: That same evening, did they say that it was the Chetniks who had shot at the tram?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: From the hospital I could not have known that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But it's you who said it. You said that same evening this piece of news had circulated and people were talking about the fact that the tram had been hit. Did the media say anything about who had done this and who had fired the shots?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I am just telling you that I was told by people who came to visit me in the hospital that I was on TV again, and it was even the subject of jokes among us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, but you must have realised that you were being filmed when you were admitted into hospital, when you came along with your girlfriend who was your girlfriend at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know whether I was being filmed. At the moment when a person is wounded and is fighting for his life, he doesn't look around, seeing whether somebody is filming him and what kind of statement he should make.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. We shall now spend a little bit more time on the police investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like my case manager to bring up on the screen document number 739, which is a Defence exhibit, which has Exhibit number D23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, the line of questioning which is not new - it's a line of questioning which you have followed - I just want to ensure that I understand your case. Your case is that, true enough, injuries were suffered by these people, but there is some doubt as to who fired the shots. The burden is on the Prosecution to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the shots came from the Serb side, and your line of questioning is directed at showing that there is some doubt as to where the shots came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in this particular example, there's another reason, but we'll come to it very rapidly. It will be demonstrated and you will understand very clearly where I am aiming at. I'm trying to introduce my own evidence so that all relative items can be discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, is there a translation into English of this latest document available that we can see?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I personally did not find the translation. Maybe the Prosecution has it. This document is included on the evidence list of the Prosecution. But it's only one sentence I want to highlight in this document, which was already used during the cross-examination of the lady who was driving the tram on that particular day. We would like it's interpreters' assistance in this matter. It starts with "On the 3rd of March ..." I would like them to translate that particular sentence which is on the screen. The witness will be able to follow on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "On the 3rd of March, 1995, at about 1210 hours, at the junction of Franjevacka Street and Marshal Tito Street, a single bullet came from a southerly direction, the neighbourhood of Grbavica, and hit tram garage number 268, moving towards Bascarsija. The tram was hit in the other part of the car between the accordion, the joint, and the third door, looking from the driver's direction. On that occasion, three persons were injured in the tram, two seriously and one slightly. The tram was being driven by driver Slavica Livnjak."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The driver of this tram testified before this Chamber. We already discussed that document on that occasion. As you can see, Witness, the police officers who examined this particular location realised that there was only one single bullet. Well, there may have been several shots, but only one bullet hits the tram. Can you see that? And, according to you, is that a true account of what happened?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I stand by my previous statements. There were two or three bullets.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In order to be even more accurate, those two to three shots that you heard, did you actually hear them or did you notice two to three bullet holes in the tram, when you left the tram with your girlfriend?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see it. I heard it and I felt it. I didn't look at the tram once I got off the tram. I just hurried over to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, could you please clarify, just to be sure, the name of the tram driver? Because I'm a bit confused from the name I see here and the name that I compare with your earlier Exhibit D23. I think I had another name there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Judge Harhoff. I believe there is a mistake here. Her name is Livnjak, Slavica. And in the whole document which follows, her name is Slavica Livnjak. So there may have been a mistake here. There's also another family name, "Polivnjak," so maybe there was some confusion between those two names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have also the name of Livnjak. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you show us the signature to that statement, the one that is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move to page 9 of that very same document. Now you can see the signature of a person named Korto Sasa. He was the technician in the Bosnian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the second page, this technician has taken note of the location where the tram was hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, it is very likely that you heard several shots. However, according to the technician, only one bullet hit the tram on that particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I was there, and I think I'm better able to say how many sounds I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But how many persons on the tram were, in fact, injured as a result of the shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I really don't know. There was a lot of panic. Everybody fell down on the floor. And I think there was another gentleman, but this is a very hazy memory, who was injured, but I didn't know at the time. There was a lot of panic. The tram reached an old building which offered relative shelter to us, and then everybody ran away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This other gentleman, was he sitting close to you or standing close to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My recollection is very hazy. I think he was seated to my right, between the third door and the joint of the tram, the middle of the tram, but I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
